title: MD5 Hash — How MD5 Works and Where It Still Applies

content.intro: MD5 produces a 128-bit (32-character hexadecimal) hash from any input. While cryptographically broken for security purposes, it remains the checksum format embedded in a huge amount of existing software, so being able to reproduce an MD5 value is still a practical skill. This guide covers what MD5 actually does and where it is still legitimate to use.

sections.heading: How MD5 Works
sections.body: MD5 processes input in 512-bit blocks through four rounds of bitwise operations, producing a fixed 128-bit output. The same input always produces the same hash, and a single bit change in the input produces a completely different hash — the avalanche effect. The output is always 32 hexadecimal characters, which is what makes the format so widely recognised.

sections.heading: Where MD5 Is Still Legitimate
sections.body: Compatibility with existing systems: many older APIs, checksum formats and build pipelines still publish MD5 digests, so being able to reproduce them matters when you are verifying or migrating data. Duplicate detection on non-adversarial content: comparing two blocks of text by digest is fast and reliable. Cache keys: content-addressed cache keys in older systems frequently use MD5. Any of these are non-security uses where collision resistance is not required.

sections.heading: Where MD5 Must Not Be Used
sections.body: Password storage: MD5 is fast, so an attacker with a stolen hash database can test billions of candidates per second. Integrity guarantees against a motivated attacker: practical MD5 collisions have been demonstrated, so two different files can share a digest. Digital signatures and certificate fingerprints: use SHA-256 or stronger. If you need to choose a single algorithm for anything new, pick SHA-256.

sections.heading: How to Reproduce an MD5 Value
sections.body: Paste or type the text into the input box and run the calculation. The Hash Tool returns MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512 side by side in hexadecimal, each with a copy button — so if you are not certain which algorithm a published checksum used, comparing it against all four outputs identifies it immediately. Everything is computed locally in your browser.

content.conclusion: MD5 is the Swiss Army knife of hashing — not the strongest algorithm, but still everywhere in existing systems. Use it for checksums and non-security hashing; for passwords and security, always choose SHA-256, SHA-512 or a purpose-built password hash.

keyTakeaways: MD5 always produces a 128-bit digest, rendered as 32 hexadecimal characters.
Still the right choice when an existing system publishes or expects an MD5 value.
Never for passwords, signatures or integrity claims against an adversary.
The Hash Tool computes MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512 from one input at once.
Runs locally in the browser — nothing is uploaded.
conclusion: MD5 is not going away — it is embedded in too much existing software to disappear. The practical rule is narrow and clear: reproduce MD5 when a system expects it, and choose SHA-256 for anything you design from scratch.
